clue.text: Booker-winning bookmaker of The Playmaker

parts.note: a 'bookmaker' here is not a turf accountant but a maker of books: the Australian novelist who won the Booker Prize for Schindler's Ark and wrote The Playmaker

explanation.surface: A racing bookie is credited with winning the Booker and producing a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bookmaker' suggests betting; it simply means an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Keneally won the 1982 Booker Prize and wrote the 1987 novel The Playmaker.

clue.text: His loves not only star-crossed, but rusticated

definitions.text: His loves not only star-crossed, but rusticated

parts.words: His loves not only star-crossed, but rusticated
parts.note: star-crossed lovers recall Romeo and Juliet; rusticated means moved to the countryside, pointing to the Swiss author of A Village Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: A man's unlucky romances have ended with him sent down from university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rusticated' tempts the student sense of being sent down; here it means set in a village.
explanation.definitionFit: Gottfried Keller wrote Romeo und Julia auf dem Dorfe, a village version of Shakespeare's tragic lovers.

clue.text: Somebody from the Grossmiths

parts.note: George and Weedon Grossmith wrote The Diary of a ___, whose diarist Charles Pooter is the classic insignificant man

explanation.surface: Someone or other is said to come from a family called Grossmith.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the 'somebody' the brothers created is famous for being the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grossmiths' comic book is The Diary of a Nobody, so their somebody is a nonentity.

clue.text: University journal

definitions.meaning: an institution of learning, the old name for an academy or college
the London literary weekly of that name, published 1828-1921

explanation.definitionFit: An athenaeum is a learned institution or academy, and The Athenaeum was a famous literary periodical.

clue.text: Poisonous plant which must have seemed funny to the Florentines

definitions.meaning: the Italian name for the mandrake, a toxic plant of folklore

definitions.text: which must have seemed funny to the Florentines
definitions.meaning: Machiavelli's comedy, first staged in Florence, carries the plant's name as its title

explanation.surface: A toxic weed somehow struck the people of Florence as amusing.
explanation.definitionFit: La Mandragola is Italian for the mandrake and is the title of Machiavelli's Florentine comedy.

clue.text: Poet's pub character?

annotationWithheld.why: Poet's pub character? (6): the source of TELFER as a character in a 'poet's pub' could not be confirmed, so no honest explanation can be given

clue.text: "One passion doth another still" (George Chapman)

parts.note: a quotation from the Jacobean dramatist with its verb missing: one passion always drives out another

explanation.surface: A line of verse from Chapman about one emotion following another.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: the missing verb completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapman's line reads 'One passion doth expel another still', meaning one feeling drives out the next.

clue.text: Novelist with 26's interests but from before Sterne

indicators.note: letters taken from within the words before Sterne, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A writer shares a fellow novelist's interests but predates Laurence Sterne.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is O'Brian, writer of sea stories; 'but from' signals the run inside 'before Sterne'.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester wrote the Hornblower naval novels, the same seafaring territory as Patrick O'Brian.

clue.text: Think again concerning Modestine

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Modestine is the donkey in Stevenson's Travels with a Donkey, a female ass, jokingly an ass-ess

explanation.surface: Someone rethinks matters involving a person called Modestine.
explanation.walkthrough: Modestine is Robert Louis Stevenson's she-donkey, so she is a female ass with the feminine ending -ESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassess is to evaluate once more, to reconsider.

clue.text: Operatic heroine named in V.s. Naipaul's The Mimic Men

definitions.text: Operatic heroine named in V.s. Naipaul's The Mimic Men

parts.words: Operatic heroine named in V.s. Naipaul's The Mimic Men
parts.note: the novel's title word Mimic begins with Mimi, the heroine of Puccini's opera, so the opera is what is meant

explanation.surface: A singer's role turns up by name in a Naipaul novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mimi sits inside 'Mimic'; the answer is the opera she belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimi is the consumptive seamstress at the heart of Puccini's opera La Boheme.

clue.text: Greek city painting in watering place

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, painting held within the watering place

parts.note: a spa is a resort with mineral springs
painting is a form of art

explanation.surface: A Greek town's picture is on show at a health resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparta was the militaristic city-state of ancient Laconia.

clue.text: Host's goriest inventions suitable for such shocking stuff

indicators.note: inventions are things made up, so the letters of the phrase are made up afresh

explanation.surface: A host's bloodiest made-up tales suit frightening fare.
explanation.definitionFit: Tales of spectres and hauntings are told to scare and shock their listeners.

clue.text: Heath encouraged, we hear (by the return of Clym Yeobright?)

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word for encouraged is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: egged on means urged or encouraged

explanation.surface: A heath is cheered on, perhaps by Hardy's hero coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: Clym Yeobright is the returning native of Hardy's The Return of the Native, set on Egdon Heath.
explanation.definitionFit: Egdon Heath is Hardy's fictional Wessex moorland.

clue.text: Nothing adequately described their beliefs

parts.note: a group whose creed is belief in nothing at all, from the Latin nihil

explanation.surface: Someone's faith was hard to put into words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' reads as 'no words could'; it is literally their creed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nihilism rejects all moral and religious principles, so its adherents believe in nothing.

clue.text: Strange relatives went hand in hand (57)

definitions.note: a phrase from Macbeth, where the witches chant 'The weird sisters, hand in hand'

parts.note: weird means strange
sisters are female relatives

explanation.surface: Odd members of a family walked along holding hands.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth the three witches go round 'hand in hand' as the weird sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's witches call themselves the weird sisters as they dance in a ring holding hands.

clue.text: Direction fit for canonized poet

parts.note: south is a compass direction
fit means healthy, well

explanation.surface: Guidance on health for a poet who was made a saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Southwell, Elizabethan Jesuit martyr and poet, was canonized in 1970.

clue.text: Prototypical drunken butler

parts.note: the tipsy servant in The Tempest who staggers ashore with a cask of wine

explanation.surface: The original sozzled servant of comic fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephano, Alonso's drunken steward in Shakespeare's The Tempest, is an early comic tippler.

clue.text: His wooing was in Stow, reportedly

definitions.text: His wooing was in Stow, reportedly

parts.words: His wooing was in Stow, reportedly
parts.note: Stow sounds like Stowe: Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote a novel about a clergyman's wooing

explanation.surface: A man's courtship is said to have taken place in a Cotswold town.
explanation.walkthrough: Stow suggests the English town; it stands for Harriet Beecher Stowe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Minister's Wooing is Harriet Beecher Stowe's 1859 novel.

clue.text: Thrice-great Neoplatonist

parts.note: the epithet of Hermes, legendary author of the Hermetic writings beloved of the Neoplatonists

explanation.surface: A philosopher hailed three times over as great.
explanation.definitionFit: Trismegistus is Greek for thrice-greatest, the title given to Hermes.

clue.text: Last resort for Francesca

parts.note: Francesca's surname in Dante is the name of an Adriatic seaside town

explanation.surface: A woman named Francesca has run out of options.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' means her final name, which is also a holiday town.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's Francesca da Rimini takes her name from the Italian beach town.

clue.text: Eliot's turbulent hero, given a bit of rope

definitions.meaning: the archbishop murdered in Murder in the Cathedral, Henry II's 'turbulent priest'
a loop or eye of rope used on ships

explanation.surface: Eliot's restless protagonist is handed some cord.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Becket is Eliot's martyred archbishop, and a becket is a nautical rope loop.

clue.text: Pale oil is mixture for the composer of I Barbiere?

indicators.note: a mixture blends things up, so the letters of the three words are blended

explanation.surface: Pale oil mixed for a composer's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Paisiello wrote Il barbiere di Siviglia (1782) before Rossini's famous version.

clue.text: Woman of Hibernia (anger not applicable)

parts.note: ire means anger

explanation.surface: An Irishwoman is described, with fury ruled out.
explanation.walkthrough: Irena is the lady in Spenser's Faerie Queene, Book V, who stands for Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's Irena personifies Ireland, Latin Hibernia.

clue.text: Writer of poems (he includes German one)

indicators.note: includes means the pronoun wraps round the German word

parts.note: taken as written
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A poet, he, takes in one German.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinrich Heine was a German lyric poet.

clue.text: A subject of Herrick's three articles

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
the is the definite article
a is the other indefinite article

explanation.surface: A Herrick topic is covered by three items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' are the grammatical kind, not essays.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Herrick addressed several poems to a mistress of that name.

clue.text: Fruit stack in verse

parts.note: a lime is a citrus fruit
a rick is a stack of hay

explanation.surface: Fruit piled up appears in a poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A limerick is a five-line comic poem.

clue.text: Novelist comes back in an air borne on the waves

indicators.note: comes back means the letters run backwards
in means the letters sit inside the words

explanation.surface: A writer returns in a song carried across the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds NAIRBO in 'an air borne' and 'comes back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick O'Brian wrote the Aubrey-Maturin sea novels.

clue.text: David changed its lamps

indicators.note: changed means the letters of the two words are altered in order

explanation.surface: David swapped the lamps around.
explanation.definitionFit: King David is traditionally credited as author of the Psalms.
